title: Given a single non-negative integer N, draw a flowchart to calculate and print N factorial (N!), the product of all integers from 1 to N inclusive. Start, read N, initialize result = 1 and i = 1, loop while i <= N doing result = result * i and i = i + 1, print result, End. Special case: 0! = 1, so the loop simply does not execute. Input: 5, Expected Output: 120.
shortTitle: Factorial: print N! as the product of all integers from 1 to N
keyPoints: Factorial of N is the product of all integers from 1 to N; by definition 0! = 1 because an empty product is the multiplicative identity.
The iterative algorithm uses a running product starting at 1 and multiplies by each integer from 1 to N.
The zero case needs no special code: the loop condition fails immediately and the product stays at 1.
Factorials overflow a Java long past 20!, so banking code uses BigInteger for exactness.
Negative input is undefined and must be rejected with IllegalArgumentException.
The time complexity is O(n) with one multiplication per step and O(1) space apart from the BigInteger itself.

s1_definition.oneliner: Factorial is a running product that starts at one and multiplies in every integer from one to N, and because an empty product is one, zero factorial is one.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Factorial (N!)** – the product of every integer from 1 up to N.
- **Zero factorial** – 0! = 1 because the product of no numbers is the multiplicative identity.
- **Running product** – initialize at 1, multiply by each counter value from 1 to N.
- **Overflow** – a Java `long` overflows past 20!; use `BigInteger` for arbitrary-precision results.
- **Negative guard** – factorial is undefined for negative numbers; reject with `IllegalArgumentException`.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India calculates how many different orders N pending cheques can be processed in. The first cheque can go in any of N slots, the next in N-1 slots, and so on down to one. Multiplying those choices is exactly N!. Rajesh asks how many ways his five cheques can be arranged, and the answer is 120.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Factorial of a non-negative integer N is the product of every integer from one up to N, and by definition zero factorial is one because the product of no numbers is the multiplicative identity. The iterative algorithm starts a running product at one, multiplies by each integer from one to N, and the zero case needs no special code because the loop condition fails immediately and the product stays at one.

The real-world subtlety for banking is overflow. Factorials grow astonishingly fast, and a Java long overflows past twenty factorial, silently producing a wrong or negative number. In a financial system that is unacceptable, so the computation uses BigInteger, which has arbitrary precision and never overflows. A guard clause rejects negative input because factorial is undefined there.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, an audit-sampling tool needed to know how many distinct orders a small batch of cheques could be processed in, which is exactly N!. The FactorialCalculator used BigInteger and validated the input. For five cheques it reported 120, and because BigInteger was used it stayed exact for much larger batches too.

Remember one sentence: seed the product at one because one is the multiplicative identity, and use BigInteger so the growing result never overflows.
